name: Iris Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at Red Hollow, the big open-pit copper mine outside Calder. Twelve-hour shifts, four on and four off, swapping between days and nights. I take ore from the shovel down to the crusher, round and round, maybe forty loads a shift. I've been there eighteen months and I'm still the one they send to the easy dump.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet in the cab at four in the morning, and the money is better than the supermarket where I used to work. What wears me out is the night swing and the new fatigue camera that beeps if I blink too long. I reversed too close to the edge at the dump last spring, and Marlene, my trainer, still watches me like a hawk. Tom, my partner, stacks shelves at night, so some weeks we only see each other on the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Half the people in the crib room thought the robots were coming next year, and I always said it's mostly talk from people selling software. Now let's talk about pay, because that's what was always the real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a relief, but it doesn't fix much. Nothing changes for the drivers, and nothing changes in my bank account either. Two weeks of rent saved is still two weeks of rent saved. Rent on our flat went up again in July, and Tom's hours at the supermarket move around every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down, same roster. Our agreement with the company is up for renewal in March, so I'd go to every union meeting and vote for the pay claim. And I'd try to put fifty a week aside until we've got a whole month of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than I've felt in a while, if I'm honest. But it's the calm of nothing changing, and nothing changing still means checking the account before the rent goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the dispatch system already plans some of the work. Would any of that change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatch screen in my cab already tells me which shovel to go to, so maybe it gets a bit smarter. Kev in the dispatch office might lose a few hours. Me, I still have to drive the thing, so I don't see it touching my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the fifty a week come out of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaway on night swing, mostly. Tom and I get chips on the way home on Thursdays, and I'd stop that. It's not much, but it's what I've got.

say: I'd tell the crib room that AI was **mostly talk**, just like I always said.
I'd say the **real fight** was always pay, not robots.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, but my money is still too thin to feel safe.
Our **rent rise** and Tom's changing hours worry me more than any machine.
Nothing in my **own cab** really changes, though dispatch might lose a few hours.
do: Keep driving the **same roster** at Red Hollow and keep my head down.
Attend every union meeting and vote for the **pay claim** in March.
Put aside **fifty a week**, starting with the Thursday takeaway.
feel: She feels **calmer**, but it's the calm of nothing changing.
Checking the account before **rent day** still sits in her stomach.
S0.quote: Nothing changes for the drivers, and nothing changes in my bank account either. Two weeks of rent saved is still two weeks of rent saved.
fieldNote: Her **union loyalty** came up before any question about technology did.
With AI off the table, her worries turn straight to **rent and pay**.
She is quietly proud of being right, a sign of how much she **distrusts the hype**.

steps.text: Keep driving the four-on four-off roster at Red Hollow
Vote for the union pay claim at the March meeting
Save fifty a week by dropping the Thursday takeaway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union meeting that we need a deal on driverless trucks before the first one turns up, not after. Other big mines already run them. I'd post that on our members' page too, because people think it's years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office goes first and the trucks come after. I'm the newest driver with a dented record, so I know whose name sits at the top of the list. The planners and the timesheet lady would feel it first, but the company would see the savings and want the same on the haul road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a clause saying no driver goes without a job offer somewhere else on site. I'd cancel the streaming and sell my old car, since Tom and I can share his. I wouldn't go chasing courses yet, because I don't know what they'd want me trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like waiting for a phone call you know is coming. I'd be angry more than scared, angry that the people who own the mine get the savings and we get the letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't chase courses yet. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company actually told us which jobs will be left, I'd train for one of them. Right now everyone says learn new skills and nobody says which ones. I'm not spending money I don't have on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev in dispatch, because his whole job is a screen. And Marlene, honestly, because she's spent fifteen years teaching people to drive, and who trains a truck that drives itself?

say: I'd tell the union we need a **driverless truck deal** before the first one arrives.
I'd post that other big mines **already run them**, so it isn't years away.
think: As the **newest driver** with a dented record, I'd expect to be cut early.
The **office goes first**, but the company will want the same savings on the haul road.
do: Push for a union clause promising every driver a **job offer** on site.
Cancel streaming and **sell my old car** to share Tom's.
Hold off on **courses** until the company says which jobs will remain.
feel: She feels like she's **waiting for a call** she knows is coming.
**Anger** at the owners outweighs fear, because they get the savings and drivers get letters.
S1.quote: The office goes first and the trucks come after. I'm the newest driver with a dented record, so I know whose name sits at the top of the list.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **office work goes first**, but still expects drivers to follow.
Her **near miss** at the dump makes her feel exposed in any cut.
She refuses to **retrain blind**, which is caution, not laziness.

steps.text: Push for a union clause guaranteeing drivers another job on site
Sell the old car and share Tom's to cut costs
Hold off on paid courses until the mine names future jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws, not promises. I'd be at every meeting, and I'd tell anyone who'd listen that the government should make the mines pay for the people they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years of warning is no warning for someone like me. I'd be 32, with a truck licence for a truck that drives itself. The dispatch office and the planners go in 2028, and three years later it's my seat. There's nothing in Calder for someone like me except the supermarket I left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd go through every bill with Tom and cut whatever we can. I'd get the union to run a campaign for a robot levy, a tax on each machine that pays for retraining, and I'd go to the local member's office myself. If it got bad, we'd move back near my mum's to save on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I like my job. I worked hard to get it, and picturing someone in an office somewhere watching my truck on a screen makes me want to throw something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes first and the robots about three years later. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd watch the office get emptied and know I'm next. Three years is just long enough to feel it coming and too short to do anything with my savings. Maybe the union could use those three years to win something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your mum's. What would that conversation with Tom sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we're adults and we can't go back to my mum's spare room. I'd say we can't pay rent on nothing. We'd probably both cry and then go anyway.

say: I'd say we need **laws, not promises**, to protect workers.
I'd tell people the government must make mines **pay for replaced workers**.
think: Two years is **no warning** for a junior driver with almost no savings.
The office goes in 2028 and **my seat** follows about three years later.
Calder has **nothing left** for me except the supermarket I left.
do: Go through **every bill** with Tom in the first month and cut hard.
Campaign for a **robot levy** and visit the local member's office.
Move back near **my mum's** if the rent can't be paid.
feel: She feels **sick** at losing a job she worked hard to get.
The image of her truck run **from a screen** makes her furious.
S2.quote: Two years of warning is no warning for someone like me. I'd be 32, with a truck licence for a truck that drives itself.
fieldNote: She grasps the **three-year gap** but sees it as dread, not breathing room.
Her plan rests on **politics and the union**, not on retraining.
Moving to **her mum's** is the real safety net, and it hurts her pride.

steps.text: Go through every household bill with Tom and cut what's possible
Campaign with the union for a robot levy to fund retraining
Visit the local member's office to argue for the levy
Move into her mum's spare room if rent becomes impossible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we've got five years to get this right, so let's not waste them. I'd want the union drawing up a plan for the drivers now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years sounds like plenty, but I know myself. I'd spend the first four telling everyone the driverless trucks will never work in our dust. That's the honest truth. I'm slow with change, and I'd hope it goes away until it obviously doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job and keep going to meetings, and I'd ask the union to set up a savings scheme through payroll so it comes out before I can spend it. Maybe I'd look at the heavy diesel fitter course at the college in a year or two, but not this year. This year I'd just try to get a proper cushion together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less like a punch, more like a weight. I'd be fine for a while, and then it'd sit on my chest on night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hope it goes away. What would tell you it isn't going away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they put a driverless test truck on the haul road, that's when. I'd see it from my cab and I'd know. That's probably when I'd sign up for something, which is probably too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fitting is hands-on too. Does that worry you, given the robots come in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I thought of that while I was saying it. Fixing the robots might last longer than driving them, but nobody can tell me how much longer. I'd still rather fix than sit at a screen.

say: I'd say the union must use the **five years** to plan for drivers.
I'd argue we shouldn't **waste the warning** this time.
think: I'd probably spend **four years** insisting driverless trucks won't cope with our dust.
I know I'm **slow with change** and would wait until it's obvious.
do: Stay in the job and keep **going to meetings**.
Ask the union for a **payroll savings scheme** so money leaves before she spends it.
Look at the **diesel fitter course**, but not in the first year.
feel: She feels it as a **weight** rather than a punch.
It would sit on her chest during **night shifts**.
S3.quote: Eight years sounds like plenty, but I know myself. I'd spend the first four telling everyone the driverless trucks will never work in our dust.
fieldNote: She is **honest about delaying**, which is unusual and revealing.
A **test truck** on the haul road is her real trigger, not the AGI date.
She prefers **fixing over screens**, even knowing fitting has limits too.

steps.text: Ask the union to set up a payroll savings scheme
Build a full month of rent through automatic payroll savings
Keep driving at Red Hollow until a driverless test truck appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where we can actually win something if we organise. Ten years is long enough to get it in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough time to fight properly. I'd want the union to win a written promise that drivers get trained into the new jobs first. I'd be about 40 when the robots come. That's young enough to start again, which is scary in its own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and put my name down for the union's technology committee, which I'd never have done before. I'd keep saving through payroll. Maybe in the first year I'd at least go to the college open day with Tom and see what the fitting course actually involves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frozen. It's the only one where I can picture myself still in Calder at 45 with a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a written promise need to say for you to trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd need names and numbers. How many drivers, which jobs, paid training on full wages, and it has to be in the agreement, not a slideshow. I've seen slideshows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 40 is young enough to start again. What would you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe something with people, like aged care, because robots doing that feels wrong to me. But I'd want to see it before I believed it.

say: I'd say this is the scenario where **organising can win** something real.
I'd argue ten years is long enough to get a **promise in writing**.
think: I'd be about **40** when robots arrive, young enough to restart.
Starting again at that age is **scary** in its own way.
do: Join the union's **technology committee** for the first time.
Visit the college **open day** with Tom to see the fitting course.
feel: It's the only scenario where she sees a **future in Calder**.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to fight properly. I'd want the union to win a written promise that drivers get trained into the new jobs first.
fieldNote: Time turns her from **defensive to organising**, a real shift for her.
She distrusts **company slideshows** and wants numbers in the agreement.
**Aged care** came up as a hopeful idea, with her own doubts attached.

steps.text: Join the union's technology committee at Red Hollow
Keep saving through payroll every fortnight
Visit the college open day to see the diesel fitting course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. What would help is a deal that's real: paid retraining on full wages while I'm still employed, and a promise of a job somewhere on site. And some income support from the government if the jobs just aren't there, because Calder can't absorb a few hundred drivers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether anyone asked us. Every time the mine brings in something new, nobody asks the people in the cab. I'm just asking to be asked before they take the cab away. The drivers know the haul road better than any engineer.

headlineQuote: Every time the mine brings in something new, nobody asks the people in the cab. I'm just asking to be asked before they take the cab away.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old haul truck driver** at a copper mine, eighteen months in and still learning.
She lives with **Tom**, who stacks supermarket shelves at night, and has about **two weeks** saved.
A loyal **union member**, she blames owners and wants laws, levies and written promises.
She avoids **new technology** and admits she'd wait until a driverless truck appears before retraining.
Her mood moves from uneasy to **alarmed** as warning time shrinks, easing only with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose her driving job around 32 with almost nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** on full wages and a promised job somewhere on site.
Government **income support** if Calder simply has no jobs left.
